title: test-0132-MAT-PROBABILITY
passage: In mathematics, the probability of an event measures how likely it is to occur, always represented as a number between 0 and 1 inclusive. An impossible event has a probability of 0, while a certain event has a probability of 1. For example, if you toss a fair coin, the probability of getting heads is 1/2, which is exactly halfway between impossible and certain. Conversely, if you have a bag with 3 red balls and 7 blue balls, the probability of picking a red ball is 3/10, not 1/2, because the outcomes are not equally likely. The sum of the probabilities of all possible elementary events in an experiment is always exactly 1. Furthermore, the probability of an event happening plus the probability of it not happening is always 1. For instance, if the probability of rain is 0.3, the probability of no rain must be 0.7. It is important to remember that as you perform more trials in an experiment, your experimental probability becomes more reliable and closer to the theoretical value. Unlike a small sample of 10 trials, 1000 trials provide a much more accurate picture of the true probability. Always ensure your final probability value never exceeds 1, as a value like 5/4 is mathematically impossible for any event.
summary: An impossible event has a 0 probability, and a certain event has a 1 probability. Furthermore, the probability of an event happening plus the probability of it not happening is always 1.
